kicker: Mutiny BIM, run end to end

scenes.text: A scan becomes a room of walls. Then a person and an agent both edit the same wall. Who wins?
scenes.say: A scan becomes a room of walls. Then a person and an agent both edit the same wall, at the same moment. Who wins?

scenes.headline: How Mutiny BIM lands an agent's edits
scenes.sub: A scan-shaped room, its IFC file, and seven races
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Corvina! I ran Mutiny BIM, modelled a room shaped like a scan's output, through an agent, and raced editors on one wall.

scenes.title: A wall is a record
scenes.sub: What the kernel stores before anyone draws it
scenes.say: Chapter one. A wall is a record.

scenes.title: One wall, as the kernel keeps it

steps.say: Every element is a plain record. A wall is a start point, an end point and a height, stored in millimetres.
It has a thickness and a type. Its class, arch dot wall, comes from the architecture add-on, not from the kernel.
steps.term: Add-on: a trade, plugged into the kernel

steps.say: A partition places it by level, zone and discipline.
And it keeps a version, plus a ledger of which fields someone wrote on purpose. That ledger decides every conflict later.
steps.term: Authored ledger: fields written on purpose

scenes.title: A scan-shaped room, from script to file

steps.say: A scan pipeline emits geometry, so here that output is a script: walls two hundred and thirty millimetres thick, a slab, a door, a window and a duct.
The preview runs it and saves nothing. Seven edit steps, with quantities a person can check against the scan.
Then the server asks a person. My first client answered without saying yes, and nothing landed.
With approval, thirteen records commit as one revision and one undo step, and every open editor sees them arrive.
Exported, the room is a valid IFC four point three file of two hundred and eighty nine entities.
The agent writes one script against the kit, and the server checks it.
Running it gives a preview: what would change, the quantities, and a hash of the output. Nothing is saved yet.
A person sees that preview and approves it. The agent cannot answer for them.
steps.term: Elicitation: the server asks the person directly

steps.say: Then the server re-runs the script, lands only what matches the preview, and commits it.

scenes.title: Tool list an agent carries
scenes.note: bytes of tool schema, measured on my run
scenes.say: That keeps the agent's context small. The core lists ten tools. With every add-on family on, it lists a hundred and sixty eight.

steps.say: Here is that loop landing. The first room is already in the plan. My client sends a second one, and approves it.
It appears in an open browser session the moment it commits.

scenes.title: Two editors, one wall
scenes.say: Chapter three. Two editors, one wall.

scenes.title: The server compares only what is recorded

params.valuesNote: By the code, element parameters share the gap: set_element_values records nothing.

steps.say: Each command tells the server which fields it wrote on purpose. A wall move records its start and its end. That is the ledger the server checks.
Two people move the same wall from the same revision. The second move is re-run on the new head, writes start differently, and is refused by name.
Now Priya sets the thickness to three hundred millimetres. The thickness command records no field at all.
A second person sets two hundred and fifty on the same base. There is nothing to compare, so both commit and the later one wins, silently.

scenes.say: So the doc's promise, no last write wins on intent, holds for moves, for people and agents. For thickness, not yet.

scenes.title: What the IFC carries
scenes.sub: Valid, and thinner than a handover
scenes.say: Chapter four. What the IFC carries.

scenes.title: What the exported room lacks
scenes.say: An open source IFC checker found the room's file valid. Reading it entity by entity, the gaps are plain.

items.say: Walls and the slab are extruded boxes. There are no materials and no common property sets.
Each wall runs from its start to its end on its centre line, so every outer corner of the room is missing a small square.
The room is an IFC space with its net floor area, and no shape a viewer can draw.
And the duct's size lives only in its profile, with no property and no flow.

steps.say: The maintainers show what a bigger script can make: plans, a single line diagram and a switchboard schedule, from one assistant's script.
That video walks through the finished model. In my run, the repository's own examples did the same at a smaller scale.

scenes.title: Where a scan fits
scenes.sub: After the walls are fitted, not before
scenes.say: Chapter five. Where a scan fits.

scenes.title: A scan-to-BIM pipeline with Mutiny in it
scenes.say: Mutiny takes no point cloud. It is where fitted elements land.

items.say: A fitting stage turns the cloud into wall lines, openings and a floor outline.
It writes them as a script, passing every measured dimension, because the defaults are in feet.
A person checks the preview against the scan and approves it.
The walls land as existing conditions, locked, and design work happens on top of them.

scenes.text: Use it as the shared model an agent edits through approvals, not yet as the IFC you hand over.
scenes.say: So use Mutiny as the shared model an agent edits through approvals. Not yet as the IFC you hand over.

recap: One script, one preview, one approval
Moves refused by name; thickness overwrites
A valid IFC, thin on data
scenes.say: To recap. One script, one preview, one approval. Conflicting moves are refused by name, but thickness overwrites. And a valid IFC that is thin on data.
